disease_info: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive worry and apprehensive expectation about multiple domains of life (e.g., work, finances, health, relationships) occurring more days than not for at least six months, and difficult for the person to control. The anxiety is typically accompanied by physical and cognitive manifestations such as restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance, leading to clinically significant distress or functional impairment. Onset is often gradual and can follow chronic stressors; the course tends to be chronic with waxing and waning severity, frequently co-occurring with depressive and other anxiety disorders. It is distinguished from normal worry by its pervasiveness, intensity, uncontrollability, and impairment, and from other anxiety disorders by the broad, non–situation-specific nature of the worry rather than being tied to discrete phobic stimuli, panic attacks, or obsessions.

narrative.personality: She is an empathetic, creatively driven young woman who juggles structured ambition with artistic side projects and a tendency to overcommit herself.
narrative.stressor: The onset of her difficulties traces back to a turbulent separation from her high school partner about a year and a half ago, which coincided with her moving out of a shared apartment and taking on full responsibility for her own bills while working in a high-pressure customer service role. Already someone who took others’ emotions to heart, she began second-guessing every decision—from whether she had chosen the right career path to whether she could realistically pursue a communications degree and UX writing certification while keeping up with rent and expectations at work. Over the following year, she increasingly filled her free time with new creative projects and volunteering to distract herself, but found that the more she tried to plan and control her future, the more mentally preoccupied she became with potential missteps in her relationships, finances, and career, leading to missed social plans and declining performance at work. She finally sought psychiatric help after her supervisor noted her growing errors and she realized that her constant mental preoccupation with “what if” scenarios about her relationships, job stability, and academic plans was making it hard to function day to day.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m constantly worrying about everything all at once, and I can’t seem to shut my mind off no matter what I do.”

narrative.personality: He is a laid-back yet curious self-taught coder who enjoys creative technical projects and community mentoring, but can be somewhat disorganized and impulsive with his lifestyle.
narrative.stressor: About fifteen months ago, his small startup lost a major client, triggering layoffs and forcing him to transition abruptly into a fully remote contract role with unstable hours and income while he scrambled to prove himself on more complex projects. Although he had previously approached coding with a relaxed, problem-solving mindset, he started to feel increasing internal pressure to match or exceed formally trained peers, worrying about every pull request, code review, and the risk of being let go if he made mistakes. Over the subsequent year, he found himself spending longer and longer evenings revisiting work, double- and triple-checking deployments, and reading about industry changes, which gradually squeezed out the balance he used to get from hiking, gaming, and mentoring students; his living space and personal finances became more disorganized as he prioritized work vigilance over everything else. He decided to seek psychiatric care when he noticed that his mind was rarely off work-related concerns, his enjoyment of hobbies had diminished, and his ability to stay focused during complex coding tasks and community teaching sessions was being undermined by a constant undercurrent of anticipatory worry about his performance and job security.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m always on edge worrying about work and my future, like my brain is stuck thinking about everything that could go wrong.”

narrative.personality: He is a highly methodical, competition-driven young technician who likes precise, hands-on projects and tends to over-plan every detail to feel in control.
narrative.stressor: His difficulties began after he left school without a diploma and quickly entered full-time work as a telecommunications line installer, a transition that felt abrupt and high stakes for someone who already relied on careful planning and structure. The combination of physically demanding work at heights, responsibility for safety and network reliability, and his ambition to earn certifications and prove himself without formal education led him to mentally rehearse every step of jobs and potential failures long before and after each shift. Over the course of the next year, this constant mental overplanning bled into other areas—he would meticulously game out contingencies for finances, transportation, and even his hobbies, spending so much time in his head that he started falling behind during actual tasks and training sessions, which only reinforced his sense that he needed to think through things even more. He ultimately sought psychiatric help when he noticed that, despite his intense preparation, he was having increasing difficulty staying mentally present during installations, making small mistakes at work, and losing the sense of enjoyment and concentration he used to have with activities like model railroading and DIY electronics because his mind kept drifting back to hypothetical problems and worst-case scenarios.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind keeps wandering and I can’t stay focused, even when I really need to concentrate at work or on projects.”
